paragraphs.heading: A small order inside a big one
paragraphs.text: A permutation pattern is a smaller permutation that sits inside a longer one. The idea belongs both to combinatorial mathematics and to theoretical computer science. To talk about patterns, we write a permutation in one-line notation: a string of entries showing where each of 1, 2, 3 and so on ends up. So 213 is the arrangement of three items in which the first two have traded places.

paragraphs.heading: What it means to contain a pattern
paragraphs.text: Take two permutations, conventionally called π and σ; here π is just a name and has nothing to do with the number pi. We say π contains σ when we can pick some entries of π whose sizes rise and fall in the same relative order as all of σ. For the pattern 213, that means finding three entries x, y and z, read left to right, where y is the smallest, x is in the middle and z is the largest. The chosen entries may sit anywhere in π; they do not have to be next to each other. Mathematicians write this containment briefly as σ ≤ π.

paragraphs.heading: Copies, and avoiding a pattern
paragraphs.text: The permutation 32415 holds the pattern 213 in five separate ways, using the entries 315, 415, 325, 324 and 215. Each of these picks is called a copy, an instance or an occurrence of the pattern. When no choice of entries works, π is said to avoid σ. For example, 51342 has ten different groups of three entries, and not a single one of them is ordered like 213, so 51342 avoids 213.

paragraphs.heading: Where the subject came from
paragraphs.text: Percy MacMahon, writing in 1915, may have proved the first result in the area. He showed that permutations which split into two decreasing subsequences, which are the ones avoiding 123, are counted by the Catalan numbers. Serious study began in 1968, when Donald Knuth looked at sorting with a stack. He proved that a stack can sort a permutation exactly when it avoids 231, and that these stack-sortable permutations are also counted by the Catalan numbers.

paragraphs.heading: Counting what avoids a pattern
paragraphs.text: A central aim of the field is to count the permutations that avoid one fixed pattern, usually a short one, or a fixed set of patterns. In the late 1980s, Richard Stanley and Herbert Wilf guessed that every pattern β comes with some constant K for which |Avₙ(β)| < Kⁿ. This guess was called the Stanley–Wilf conjecture until Adam Marcus and Gábor Tardos proved it.

paragraphs.heading: Finding a pattern by computer
paragraphs.text: The matching problem asks whether a pattern of length k shows up in a given permutation of length n, which here is called the text. If both lengths are allowed to grow, the problem is NP-complete, and counting all the matches is #P-complete. Yet when k is held fixed, the question can be answered in time that grows only in step with n. Since 2003, researchers in the area have gathered each year at a conference called Permutation Patterns.
